How the system connects

Minnesota disability services are state-supervised and county-administered. The Department of Human Services sets policy and pays for services; the Disability Services Division leads the disability programs; lead agencies assess people and manage their services; and licensed providers deliver them. This page shows how those parts connect, with a source for each point.

Equity Activity Inventory

The central registry of equity work, described in the One DSD proposal as the “central nervous system” for coordination.⁴ Before starting something new, teams check whether related work exists, who owns it, what was learned and whether collaboration is possible.

Operating rules

Governance charter

A charter makes the framework operational by clarifying who decides, who advises, who carries out work and how concerns move upward. Meeting patterns are set by the members; none are fixed here.

Equity, accessibility and decision tools

Equity Analysis Toolkit

Run an equity analysis before a significant decision, not after implementation has begun. The State of Minnesota toolkit and the DHS Equity Policy describe it as a way to examine how decisions affect different groups, prevent unanticipated harm and address persistent racial disparities that routine decisions can otherwise reproduce.⁵ In this program the guided walkthrough carries the questions, keeps a record and counts the result on the Equity Policy dashboard.

Accessibility review checklist

Accessibility is a design requirement, not a last-minute accommodation. The Americans with Disabilities Act and Section 508 are the legal foundations; this program holds itself to WCAG 2.2 Level AA.⁶

Minimum standard for every major initiative

Inclusive hiring and workforce equity toolkit

Supports workforce equity, retention, equitable advancement and workplace culture.⁷ Data in this kit is analyzed at the group level; the program holds no personnel records.

Community, learning and culture tools

Community engagement toolkit

Engagement is reciprocal partnership rather than information extraction: plan early, reduce participation barriers, compensate expertise and show how feedback changed decisions.⁸ Minnesota Communities carries the program’s reviewed community context.

{LEADING_LABEL}

{LEADING_LABEL}

How this works

What is recorded, what is not, and what this space does not do.

There is no team view

{LEADING_PRIVACY_SENTENCE}

  • There is no sign-in for this space. All of it is public, and staff can read every page.
  • There is no team view, no assignments and no scores.
  • A supervisor cannot see who opened a course, how far they got or what they answered. Neither can you.

What stays in your browser

  • Your progress stays in your browser. That includes your place on a suggested path, your lesson progress and your practice answers.
  • Nothing is sent to a supervisor or employer.
  • Anyone using the same computer and browser could see it. You can clear it at any time.

What happens to a question in Ask

  • Questions typed into Ask go to outside services so that it can answer.
  • The current service does not intentionally save a question-and-answer copy in the owner workspace. Operational activity may be recorded, and earlier versions may have retained separate records. Supervisors do not receive your browser conversation from Ask.
  • Please do not type anyone's name, case, health or personnel details. Ask general questions.

What this does not replace

  • This app does not replace training the state requires. It does not count as the training Minn. Stat. 43A.21 requires of supervisors and managers. The state's own training does that.
  • It is general information, not legal advice. For a real situation, ask Human Resources, labor relations or your ADA coordinator.
  • It does not make or record any personnel, accommodation or complaint decision.

The one exception to voluntary use

{TRAINING_CREDIT_NOTICE}

The Equity Analysis Toolkit is required of all staff of the Minnesota Department of Human Services, regardless of status, so it is marked “{REQUIRED_COURSE_LABEL}” wherever it is listed here. This app does not assign it or report on who has taken it. Open the Equity Analysis Toolkit course.

Using the learning

Use these courses as guidance for your work, alongside current policy and the people and offices responsible for a decision.

Tribal and Native American learning

This space does not offer Tribal curriculum. One DSD refers Native American and Tribal-specific learning, questions and engagement to ADSA and the responsible Tribal liaison. Native American and Tribal-specific guidance.

{LEADING_LABEL}

Optional

Your leadership journey

A way to grow as a leader at your own pace, from a first interest in leading to setting direction for others.

There is no nomination, no group to join and no deadline. You choose where to start and how fast to go. {LEADING_PRIVACY_SENTENCE} How this works.

How one round works

Each round is small: one lesson, a few lines of reflection, one thing tried in your real work, and a note on what happened. Then you go around again.

    {JOURNEY_STEPS.map(step =>
  1. {step.title}. {step.body} {step.link}.
    2. )}

Most of what makes someone a better leader comes from trying things in real work. Some comes from other people: a colleague, a mentor, a team. A small part comes from lessons. So the lessons here are short, and each one leads to something to try.

Find a starting point

Answer two or three questions about your work, or simply choose from the list below.

    {LEADING_PATHS.map(path =>
  • {path.title} {PATH_JOURNEY[path.slug] ? {PATH_JOURNEY[path.slug].question} : {path.description}} Open this path
    • )}

A steady rhythm

A week that fits inside real work looks something like this. Take less when the week is full.

    {WEEKLY_RHYTHM.map(item =>
  • {item.what}: {item.time}
    • )}
One way to pace a path over six weeks
    {SIX_WEEKS.map(week =>
  1. Week {week.week}. Learn: {week.learn}. Reflect: {week.reflect}. Apply: {week.apply}.
    2. )}

This is one example. Any path can be taken faster, slower or in a different order.

Looking back

Reflection is what turns a lesson into a change. A few lines are enough, and three questions carry most of it: what happened, why it matters, and what you will do next. Open your reflection notebook.

    {REFLECTION_PROMPTS.map(prompt =>

    • )}

Learning with others, if you want to

None of this is required. A conversation with someone you trust can deepen what you notice.

    {LEARNING_WITH_OTHERS.map(place =>
  • {place.title}{place.body}
    • )}

For anyone who wants more. These belong to other organizations, open on their sites, and may ask you to create an account there. They do not count toward required training unless your manager, director or agency leadership approves an exception.

    {LEARNING_ELSEWHERE.map(course =>

    • )}

At the end of a path

Four questions to ask yourself:

    {END_OF_PATH_QUESTIONS.map(question =>
  • {question}
    • )}

“The notice was sent.” This records an activity. It does not establish understanding or accessibility.

Turn one idea into one change you can see at work. Name a small first step, a real moment to try it, and a date thirty days out to look back.
values.field1: Why a plan this small works
values.field2: Change sticks when it is specific, tied to a moment you already face and reviewed soon after. A single behavior you try three times teaches more than a long list you never start. The review questions help you separate what you observed from what you hoped, and decide whether to keep, adjust or stop.

values.field1: For decisions that reach people through a rule, a form, a budget or a service.
values.field2: Name the problem before you solve it
values.field3: Connect the decision to its purpose. Ask what the work is trying to achieve, what stands in the way and whose experience can inform the problem. Use evidence to decide what to change.
values.field4: Clarify the decision and who holds it
values.field5: Explain what can be decided, who has authority, and where input is needed before a decision is made.
values.field6: Before inviting people to participate, explain what can be influenced, when a decision will be made and how people will hear what happened.
values.field7: Look for barriers in routine practices, such as meeting times, forms, communications and access to information.
values.field8: For how people are brought in, supported, heard and kept.
values.field9: Agree on clear ways of working, explain what they look like in practice and revisit them with the team. People can contribute in different ways, including speaking, writing or a one-to-one conversation.
values.field10: Give notice and several ways to participate
values.field11: Share materials early, explain the purpose and offer more than one way to respond. Ask what perspectives or information are missing.
values.field12: Give supervisors time, relevant information and support to carry out changes, and invite feedback from people affected.
values.field13: Examine access to information, opportunities, decisions and support as well as representation. Ask which routines may create barriers.
values.field14: People grow. Leadership grows with them.
values.field15: Grow your equity leadership
values.field16: Bring your experience, your curiosity, and the kind of leader you want to become. Develop a practice that makes equity, inclusion, and accessibility part of how DSD works.
values.field17: Explore equity in the practice of leadership—whether you are discovering your potential, supporting a team, or shaping the division's future.

values.field20: Teams and the organization
values.field21: Connect culture with leadership practice
values.field22: Reflect on how your perspective shapes policy, program and resource decisions as well as hiring, development and workplace culture. Explore community context while asking people what matters to them.
values.field23: Explore Cultural Intelligence
values.field24: Lead the team and the organization
values.field25: Use these practical questions when a decision involves policy, programs, services, workforce or workplace culture. Consider the people affected, applicable responsibilities and more than one perspective. Check whether a change helps in the actual situation.
values.field26: Keep learning separate from personnel decisions
values.field27: Cultural intelligence and the Intercultural Development Inventory are learning resources, not scores or labels for hiring, promotion, ratings or performance reviews. Supervisors and Human Resources retain their responsibilities under the applicable processes.
values.field29: Diversity, equity, inclusion, and accessibility shape how we interpret experience, distribute opportunities, and make decisions. This One DSD experience connects learning with the employee life cycle, with room to examine assumptions and improve the conditions in which people work.
values.field30: Lead equity through the employee life cycle
values.field31: From role design and recruitment to development, retention, and succession, each stage offers a practical way to grow. Use these situations to explore the capability you chose in your development map.
values.field32: This voluntary learning experience has no minimum service requirement. Choose a question that fits your role and interests. Formal training programs and job opportunities have their own requirements.
values.field33: For a supervisor considering a director role, a useful roadmap begins with the role's responsibilities: compare them with demonstrated experience, choose a supported practice opportunity, seek feedback, and build examples of what changed. Advancement also depends on the applicable qualifications and selection process.
values.field36: A conversation with a mentor or sponsor
values.field37: Bring your development map. Discuss the capability you want to practice, an opportunity that fits, the time and access you need, and how you will receive feedback. Mentoring can help you think through the experience; sponsorship can help make an opportunity available.
values.field39: What did you observe me do, and what difference did it make?
values.field40: Whose perspective or access did the approach make room for?
values.field41: Where did an assumption or a working condition get in the way?
values.field42: What could I try differently next time?
values.field43: You can also bring a question to a trusted colleague. Agree on what may be shared, and focus feedback on the work and its effects.
values.field44: A personal development map can connect with a wider continuity need. When colleagues can practice critical work with support, they build experience while the division strengthens its ability to carry that work forward.
values.field45: What meaningful progress could look like
values.field46: A clearer aspiration, an opportunity they can access, a skill they have practiced, useful feedback, and a work example they can explain. Growth may mean greater contribution in a current role as well as interest in advancement.
values.field47: Clearer criteria, more accessible development opportunities, follow-through on staff feedback, and critical work that more than one person can carry forward. Examine appropriate aggregate patterns with the responsible partners; course completion alone cannot show these outcomes.
values.field48: Connected with the whole One DSD program
values.field49: Reflection becomes richer when it connects with another perspective. Bring a practice question to the One DSD Team, explore mentoring through Amplify, or follow a resource into the wider program.
values.field51: These references informed this original program experience. Examples are learning situations, not accounts of named staff.

A shared understanding

{OPERATIONALIZING_EQUITY.definition}

This program definition draws on DHS equity policy, Minnesota’s equity-analysis guidance and the GARE approach. The original sources are linked below.

Knowledge, relationships and practical action

Cultural awareness, intercultural learning, relationship-building, social justice, restorative practice and structural analysis offer connected ways to understand and advance equity. Each can contribute useful perspectives to the work people share.

Operationalizing equity brings attention to how that understanding informs a particular decision or practice. It invites people to examine who can participate, how resources and opportunities are distributed, and what helps an approach work well in its setting.

Structural inequities concern patterns in policies, processes and institutions that create or sustain unequal access and opportunity. Examining those patterns helps people identify practical points for change. The focus is on understanding how the work functions and considering its effects.

Different situations call for different knowledge and support. Professional experience, community knowledge, respectful inquiry and evidence all have a place. Racial equity, disability access, language access and other dimensions may intersect; learning directly from people helps clarify what matters in a particular situation.

For a policy or service question, begin with the applicable requirements and available evidence. DHS equity policy provides policy context; the responsible office clarifies which requirements apply to the work.

Community knowledge can help you prepare thoughtful questions and identify perspectives to seek. Use the equity review tools to examine effects, compare alternatives and prepare a recommendation that makes uncertainties and needed decisions visible.

After the appropriate decision and implementation, measurement guidance and practice reflection help you distinguish what was done from what changed. Return what you learn to the people who contributed and to the next analysis. No tool substitutes for their participation or for authorized review.

How this program operates

The Program charter connects the purpose, operating principles, consultant responsibilities, authority boundaries and evidence needed to carry work forward. It guides the whole program, including equity work beyond the ADSA implementation plan.

Use the requirements and review evidence workspace to identify applicable requirements, connect them with sources and prepare evidence for the person responsible. A prepared document does not establish approval or implementation.

Where an ADSA action step applies, the six-goal implementation map connects it with practical work products, participation, tools and questions about results. Divisions can adapt their approach to their responsibilities; these twenty-eight steps do not limit the program’s broader equity work.

Keep learning from experience

Completing a course or preparing a document is a starting point. Notice how you use it, whose experience informs your decisions, and what becomes different in practice. What you learn may lead to a new question or a different approach.

Leadership learning: from awareness to accountable action

These four connected lessons are for leaders, supervisors, managers and directors. Explore them in any order. Each uses a fictional DSD example to consider leadership, power, access and organizational change. Take notes in your own preferred format; this page does not collect responses or score people. Do not include identifiable case, medical or personnel details in an informal exercise.

Leadership approaches and the decisions they shape

Leadership is part of cultural understanding and organizational change. Leaders, supervisors, managers and directors can use these approaches to examine their own decisions and responsibilities. These approaches describe ways people may lead; they are not labels, scores or a complete list. A person can use different approaches in different situations. Consider what is needed, who has authority, who can influence the decision, and what happens for the people affected.

Bring the comparison to DSD work

In a service decision or workplace change, ask: Whose experience shapes the problem? Who has the authority to change the process? Can people disagree without retaliation? How do race, gender, disability, language, income and other circumstances affect access and influence? Ask people what works for them; do not assume a person speaks for a whole community.

For example, a supervisor, manager and director supporting a team updating a notice could clarify their respective decisions, set a clear safety deadline, invite disabled people and communities affected to identify access barriers, share which choices are open, and report back on changes. Compare the approach taken with the effect on participation and the decision—not with a score on a leader.

Leadership research uses these terms in different ways, and evidence from one setting does not prove an outcome in another. Use this comparison for reflection and discussion, alongside applicable policies and responsibilities.

values.field31: Read, reflect and examine the organization
values.field32: Anti-racism asks how racial inequities are produced and sustained through decisions, authority, resources and everyday practices. These readings connect the Anti-Racism Resource Guide to the six goals. They are companion learning, not an assessment or a score of staff.
values.field33: Institutional structures: look beyond an individual interaction
values.field34: An interaction may reveal a barrier, but the cause can also lie in a requirement, a deadline, access to information or the way decisions are authorized. A uniform rule can have different effects when people have unequal access to time, money, language support or established networks. Examine both the immediate experience and the routine that shapes it.
values.field35: For example, training staff to explain a complex application may improve an interaction while leaving its burden intact. Reviewing which steps are necessary, who can change them and how alternatives affect people addresses the institutional process. Useful action can combine learning, an authorized change and feedback from people who use the process.
values.field36: Choose one requirement in your selected goal. Describe its intended purpose, who carries its burden, the evidence you need and the role with authority to change it.
values.field37: Tokenism: connect representation to influence and support
values.field38: Representation matters, but an invitation does not establish meaningful participation. People may be visible in a meeting, a campaign or an entry-level workforce while having little influence over priorities, resources or advancement. Tokenism can also place a disproportionate burden on someone expected to explain or represent an entire community.
values.field39: Ask what participants can change, whether different perspectives can disagree safely, what support makes participation possible and how decisions will be reported back. In hiring and retention, consider opportunity and everyday treatment after recruitment. In communication, connect inclusive messages to usable information and responsive practice.
values.field40: Before inviting input, state one decision that remains open and how contributors can affect it. Afterward, show what changed, what did not and why.
values.field41: Organizational culture: sustain change through everyday practice
values.field42: Stated values become credible through recurring choices: who gets time to learn, whose evidence is considered, who can pause a decision, and what happens when someone names a barrier. A training or policy statement is a starting point. Sustained change also needs resources, accountable roles, changed routines and opportunities to learn from effects.
values.field43: The guide presents an organizational action continuum for examining patterns of exclusion, symbolic inclusion, structural change and sustained anti-racist practice. Different practices can show different patterns. Use it to ask better questions about a specific practice and its evidence; do not assign staff a label or infer their intercultural orientation.
values.field44: The Intercultural Development Inventory (IDI) and the organizational continuum serve different purposes. This companion neither administers those instruments nor substitutes its reflection for qualified interpretation.
values.field45: Compare a stated commitment with a recurring decision. Identify what support, authority and review would make the commitment more consistent in practice.

values.field48: , sections on institutional and structural action, organizational culture, tokenism and the organizational action continuum. The guide cites Ed Schein (2004) on culture and attributes the continuum to Crossroads Ministry, adapted from Bailey Jackson and Rita Hardiman, developed further by Andrea Avazian and Ronice Branding, and adapted by Melia LaCour, PSESD. This is a program synthesis of the source guide, not a new DHS policy or a validated organizational finding.

Write the four lines

Use “Notes to take with you” below to draft your response. Separate what the scene tells you from what you would need to ask.

  1. What happened? Record the arrival time and request without assigning a motive.

See a practice handover and readiness check

A team wants more than one colleague to be able to prepare a recurring review. The example follows the work and its decision points.

Critical work
Prepare a monthly list of unresolved cross-team handoffs for the process owner to review.
Capability needed
Distinguish a missing update from an unresolved decision and direct each question to the right role.
Open opportunity
Invite interested colleagues to shadow and then co-prepare one review, with agreed time, accessible materials and feedback.
First handover
A checklist names the files and the sequence, but does not explain when the process owner must decide.
Readiness check
A colleague tries a practice case. They find the files but cannot tell who may resolve the exception. That identifies a gap in the handover, rather than establishing a lack of potential.
Revise and test
Add the decision boundary and the responsible role, then repeat the walkthrough. Keep appropriate process knowledge in the approved workplace location.

values.field22: Keep the person's work goal in the comparison
values.field23: An invented job seeker says they enjoy organizing information and want paid work with a local business. Their expressed interest starts the discussion.
values.field24: Begin with the available service slot
values.field25: “There is an opening in the current day program.” Availability answers a scheduling question, but does not yet explore the person's employment goal.
values.field26: Discuss the tasks the person wants to try, relevant paid employment possibilities and the support or access arrangements they request.
values.field27: Connect a family's question to a clear follow-up
values.field28: A practice family calls about children's services, requests a particular language and asks how to find out about provider availability. The map concerns access and follow-through, not clinical advice.
values.field29: Ask what the family wants to understand and confirm the language and communication support they request.
values.field30: Explain the planning conversation and the information that will be discussed in an accessible format.
values.field31: Identify who will check the provider question and how the family can reach that person or role.
values.field32: Offer support for a decision without taking it over
values.field33: In an invented planning conversation, a person asks for more time and a written explanation of two options. They also choose someone to help them discuss the information.
values.field34: “This seems complicated, so we will choose for you.” The response assumes that needing support settles who should decide.
values.field35: “How would you like us to explain the options, and what help would you like while considering them?” Check understanding and the person's preferred next step.
values.field36: Trace a requirement before it screens someone out
values.field37: Imagine a draft grant application asks applicants to list several previous state contracts. Follow the requirement back to the capability the work actually needs.
values.field38: Describe the work a successful provider must be able to do, such as delivering a service in the required languages and formats.
values.field39: Consider whether a work example, relevant community experience or another permitted form of evidence can demonstrate the same capability.
values.field40: Bring the proposed criteria and reporting expectations to procurement and contract owners before the solicitation is settled.
values.field41: Connect an equity commitment to a decision
values.field42: In this example, a team wants translated information to be available when a program change begins. A general commitment becomes useful when the decision, capacity and response are clear.
values.field43: Identify the vital information, the people who need it and the decision date that shapes the work.
values.field44: Identify who can decide, what translation and review capacity is needed and what tradeoffs remain open.
values.field45: Tell the team what was decided, what remains unresolved and when it can be reconsidered.
values.field46: Compare an impression with job-related evidence
values.field47: Imagine this position requires explaining service options clearly and coordinating a handoff. Those are practice duties for examining the screening problem; the actual role still needs its own review.
values.field48: “The answer was confident, and the graduate degree feels reassuring.” Neither observation yet states how the candidate demonstrated the agreed work.
values.field49: “In the work example, the candidate explained two options, checked understanding and identified who would follow up.” Compare that evidence with the same written criteria for each candidate.
values.field51: These two supervisor responses show the difference between general encouragement and a concrete development conversation.
values.field52: “Keep doing good work. Your time will come.” The response leaves the next role, access to visible work and the employee's question unexplained.
values.field53: “Let's identify what the next role requires and what experience you already bring. We can discuss an openly offered project opportunity and take classification questions to HR.”
values.field54: Keep access connected across the rotation
values.field55: Follow the points where responsibility can disappear. The handoff concerns agreed arrangements, not an employee's diagnosis or private personnel information.
values.field56: Include access information with the rotation invitation for everyone. Identify the role responsible for confirming arrangements before the move.
values.field57: Plan captions, advance material and an alternative to activities that require speed. Ask participants which arrangements they need.
values.field58: Ask whether the arrangements are working and respond to a missing support promptly through the appropriate route.
values.field59: Give the same next step more than one usable route
values.field60: A self-service step can be one choice. This practice access map keeps a real human route and a person's chosen support in view from the start.
values.field61: A person who chooses it can use an accessible form, find help and understand what follows.
values.field62: A staffed phone or in-person option can reach the same purpose without requiring the person to first fail online.
values.field63: Ask who the person wants involved and what would make the decision understandable.
values.field64: Every route ends with a usable explanation of the next step and the person or role responsible for follow-up.
values.field65: Put the invitation on the decision timeline
values.field66: The decision in the scenario is approved and funded. A listening invitation should explain what remains open instead of implying influence that no longer exists.
values.field67: Another unit asked similar questions last year. Recover the purpose, commitments and unanswered report-back before asking again.
values.field68: Identify the decisions already made and the authority needed to revisit any of them.
values.field69: Explain the settled decision, any implementation choices still open, how input can affect them and how people will hear the response.
values.field70: This made-up four-part response follows listening about a meeting invitation. It demonstrates specificity without inventing a commitment about the program in the scenario.
values.field71: “The reply instructions were hard to find, and a daytime discussion did not work for some participants.” Use a checked theme; quote a participant only with appropriate permission.
values.field72: “The draft invitation now puts the reply action first and offers a written contribution route.” Describe an actual change only after it has been made.
values.field73: “An additional meeting time still needs an organizer and available capacity.” Explain the real constraint instead of promising the option.
values.field74: Name the contact role, the next opportunity to influence the work and the agreed time to return with an answer.
values.field75: Repair the form and the route to using it
values.field76: This comparison describes the form problem without asking anyone to complete an inaccessible demonstration. The same required information should be usable through an accessible route.
values.field77: Text and blanks appear only as a picture. The person cannot navigate labeled fields, review the reading order or correct an error with a screen reader.
values.field78: Headings explain the sections; every field has a programmatic label; instructions and errors are stated in text; keyboard navigation follows the task.
values.field79: Move language access to the first contact
values.field80: These English text examples describe the service arrangement. They are not translated greetings or a substitute for qualified interpretation.
values.field81: An English-only message asks the caller to leave information. Language support is available only after someone calls back.
values.field82: A route to a supported conversation
values.field83: A usable first-contact route helps the caller state the language they request and reach a staff member with qualified interpretation. Staff explain what happens next and check understanding.
values.field84: Connect ways to contribute with visible influence
values.field85: This practice meeting sequence changes the process around contribution. It does not explain why any particular colleague is quiet.
values.field86: Share the decision and material in advance. Offer a written route so ideas need not compete for a fast speaking turn.
values.field87: Bring written and spoken contributions into the same discussion. The supervisor leaves room before adding their own view.
values.field88: Explain what changed, what did not and why. Credit contributions appropriately and say what remains open.
values.field89: A leader can name the problem and change the next step
values.field90: These practice responses address the unchallenged generalization in the scenario. They do not ask affected staff to explain or represent a community.
values.field91: “We know nobody meant anything by it. Let's move on.” The response centers an assumed intention and leaves the claim unexamined.
values.field92: “I should have paused that generalization. It does not tell us what this person or family wants. Let's identify the evidence we need and the question we should ask.”
values.field93: Separate the safeguard from the waiting
values.field94: A practice decision record can make a stalled approval discussable without assuming the step can simply be bypassed.
values.field95: Find what risk the approval step was meant to address and the evidence that it still needs this treatment.
values.field96: Name the role with authority to retain, revise or remove the step and what that role needs to decide.
values.field98: Describe another way to address the risk, its resources and limits, and the point at which results would be reviewed.

values.field0: A notice points to one contact. The staff instructions point to another. Name the mismatch without guessing why it happened.
values.field1: The team compares the two instructions and drafts a clearer first contact, next step, and fallback for discussion.
values.field2: The service owner considers the proposal with the people responsible for the handoff. Agree what can change and what needs more work.
values.field3: Follow a confusing handoff through
values.field4: A useful contribution connects a question with evidence, a person who can decide, and a response to the people who raised it.
values.field5: Return to the people who contributed
values.field6: Share the response, including what remains open. If something changes, return to whether it helped. If no change is agreed, explain that too.
values.field7: Read the example work note

values.field0: A meeting can make room for a second perspective
values.field1: Check the explanation through the next action
values.field2: Trace a renewal notice beyond its wording
values.field3: Compare the evidence before claiming improvement
values.field4: Explore the example more closely
values.field5: Two moments of one meeting: on the left four colleagues talk around a table; on the right the same colleagues write on response cards.
values.field6: Two ways to contribute: conversation and time to write. Neither photograph shows whether an idea influenced the decision. The facilitator still needs to bring the contributions into the discussion and explain what changed.
values.field7: Practice employment-planning example
values.field8: Follow one contribution through the decision
values.field9: If the phone route is proposed but has no confirmed owner, describe it as unresolved. A contribution becomes influence when an actual choice changes.

Make the next action easy to find

Compare two versions of a made-up workshop notice. The revision keeps the choices, reply date and offer of support while changing how a reader finds them.

First draft

In order to facilitate the finalization of arrangements for the forthcoming workshop, participants are requested to communicate their preferred session (morning or afternoon) to the workshop team by October 18. Revised draft

Choose a workshop time. Reply by October 18.

See how one meeting change can lead to learning

In this example, a team wants colleagues to have a meaningful chance to shape a decision.

  1. Before: open the question

  3. After: show what changed

    The team shares the decision, the input that shaped it and questions still open. Colleagues can check whether the account reflects what they contributed.

values.field5: Turn the lens toward our own institution
values.field6: This course examines how historically dominant white cultural norms in American and Minnesota institutions can shape what seems normal, credible or fair. It connects that examination to community perspectives, disability and language access, intercultural communication, workforce decisions and leadership responsibility.
values.field7: Cultural patterns are a starting point for inquiry. They do not tell us what any individual believes or needs. Responsive practice combines evidence, direct listening and a willingness to change how the organization works.
values.field8: By the end, you will be able to
values.field9: Identify assumptions in a service or workplace decision and distinguish evidence from interpretation.
values.field10: Use community perspectives and cultural briefs to ask better questions without stereotyping people.
values.field11: Choose a practical organizational response, identify who can act and decide how to check whether access improves.
values.field12: Dates and scope matter. Historical findings provide context; they are not presented as current DHS statistics.
